title: Python Basics Checkpoint
intro: You have learned print, variables, data types and math. Time to prove it. Eleven rounds, one from every idea in this module. Get them right on the first try to earn ⭐⭐⭐!

rounds.prompt: Run this line. What shows up on the screen?
rounds.explain: print shows whatever is inside the quotation marks. The quotes themselves are not printed.

rounds.prompt: This line is broken. Pick the fix.
options: Add the missing closing quote: print("Coding is fun")
Swap the brackets for curly ones
Add a number at the end
rounds.explain: Every opening quote needs a closing quote. Without it Python keeps looking for where the text ends and runs off the line.

rounds.prompt: Which line stores the number 7 in a variable called score?
rounds.explain: The name goes on the left of the equals sign and the value goes on the right. Python reads it as: put 7 into score.

rounds.prompt: A variable can be given a new value. What does this print?
rounds.explain: The second line replaces the value. Python keeps only the newest one, so lives holds 1 by the time print runs.

rounds.prompt: What kind of data is "42" (with the quotation marks)?
options: A string, because of the quotes
An int you can do math with
rounds.explain: Quotation marks make a value text, even when it looks like a number. Without the quotes, 42 would be an int.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a valid boolean in Python?
rounds.explain: A boolean is written True or False with a capital letter. Lowercase true is not defined, and "True" in quotes is a string, not a boolean.

rounds.prompt: Careful with division. What does this print?
rounds.explain: The / operator always gives a decimal answer in Python. 10 divided by 4 is 2.5. If you wanted the whole-number part only, you would use //.
The % operator gives what is left over after dividing. 3 goes into 7 twice with 1 left over, so the answer is 1.

rounds.prompt: Order of operations. What does this print?
rounds.explain: Multiplication happens before addition, so Python works out 3 * 4 first to get 12, then adds 2. Wrapping (2 + 3) in parentheses would give 20 instead.

rounds.prompt: Match each Python piece to what it does.

pairs.right: Puts a value into a variable

rounds.explain: These six pieces cover everything in this module: showing output, storing values, and the four basic data types.

rounds.prompt: Build the program: store a price, store a tax, add them up, then show the total.
rounds.explain: Create each variable before you use it. The third line reads price and tax, adds them, and stores the answer in total. Only then can print show it.
